title: Bernard on love
hookLine: we love ourselves, then God for ourselves, then God for God, and at last ourselves for God

cards: A small girl visits her grandmother because there are cookies. That's the honest truth of it. Years later she still visits, but now it's for the grandmother: the stories, the laugh, the hands.
Later still, long after the cookies stopped mattering, she notices something odd. Loving her grandmother changed how she loves herself.
A monk wrote a whole ladder of love along those lines, except the one he was climbing toward was God. His name was Bernard.

teach.b: Bernard was a Cistercian abbot at a monastery called Clairvaux. Someone asked him why God should be loved, and how much.
His answer opens his little book On Loving God: the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is to love without measure. Then he sets out a ladder.
At first, he says, we love ourselves, for our own sake. That's where people begin, and he doesn't scold it. Then trouble comes, and we turn to God for help.
Now we love God, but still for what God gives. Bernard counts that as real love, a true step up. Keep coming back, and something shifts.
You begin to taste how good God is, and you love God not for what you get but because God is good.
The first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, puts the root of it plainly: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us."
The top rung is the strangest: you love even yourself only for God's sake.
Bernard isn't sure anyone fully reaches it in this life; he wonders aloud whether it waits for the next.
Elsewhere, preaching on the Song of Songs, he says love needs no reward beyond itself: I love because I love. The ladder starts with need and ends in love that asks for nothing back.

how: Catholics honor Saint Bernard of Clairvaux as a Doctor of the Church; his On Loving God and his sermons on the Song of Songs are read in monasteries and by people making retreats, and his feast is kept in late summer.

o: an abbot who mapped love's climb toward God
a king who gave his castle to the monks
a monk who founded the first abbey in France

p: loving ourselves for our own sake
loving God for what God gives

s: Bernard said God should be loved in moderation
the measure of loving God, he wrote, is to love without measure.
Bernard's ladder of love begins with loving ourselves
the first degree is loving oneself for one's own sake; he doesn't scold it.
Bernard thought the top rung was easy to reach
he wondered whether anyone fully reaches loving themselves only for God's sake in this life.

games.q: you notice you mostly pray when you need something. what would Bernard say?
o: that isn't love at all; stop.
that's a real rung on the ladder; keep climbing.
games.why: Bernard counts loving God for what God gives as a true degree of love, and says coming back again and again can lead to loving God for God's sake.

practice: Choose one thing you love: a person, a place, a piece of music, the light in a certain window.
Notice how much of the love is about what it gives you, which is where Bernard starts too, then try, for a moment, to love it simply because it's good.
If you pray, let that turn toward God, who, the letter of John says, loved first.

wordCard.voice: Bernard. The Cistercian abbot whose ladder of love rises from loving ourselves to loving God for God's sake, and at last, ourselves for God. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: love for love's sake. The ladder starts wherever you are. Day eight hundred two, done.
